description: The only official music video Phish ever made — four guys in scuba gear, swimming through an aquarium toward their own New Year's Eve stage.

pops.text: This is it — the only official music video Phish ever produced. Bassist Mike Gordon directed it himself in 1994.
The band spends the clip in scuba gear, diving through a giant aquarium — then surfaces onto the stage of their own 1993 New Year's Eve show, which was aquarium-themed.
The first single from Hoist (1994), the song was Phish's first to chart — it hit #33 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks that summer.
The video got airplay on MTV, and even appeared on Beavis and Butt-Head. The cartoon duo, reportedly, was not impressed.
The lyrics came from real life: Tom Marshall's bout with mononucleosis gave the song its germy title.
Phish first played it at midnight on New Year's Eve 1993 — as a wordless jam melting out of 'Auld Lang Syne.' The full song didn't arrive until April 1994.
Hoist was recorded in late 1993 in Woodland Hills, California with producer Paul Fox — Phish's deliberate, guest-packed bid for a wider audience.
The album features Alison Krauss, Béla Fleck, Tower of Power's horn section, and Star Trek actor Jonathan Frakes on trombone.
To promote Hoist, Gordon also directed Tracking, an experimental short film about the recording sessions.
Live, 'Down with Disease' became a jam vehicle — the longest standalone version, from December 1995, runs over 31 minutes.

title: Down with Disease

description: Phish's 1994 bid for the radio dial — a drunken-seatbelt ballad with cryptic lyrics, captured live at their legendary Clifford Ball festival.

pops.text: The second single from Hoist — Phish's 1994 attempt to make a real, radio-friendly record.
It was cut in late 1993 at the American Recording Company in Woodland Hills, California, with producer Paul Fox.
Trey once summed the song up bluntly: it's about 'sitting in a car with the seatbelt on, drunk.'
The strange lyrics name Elihu and Leemor — characters from a private mythology Trey and Tom Marshall had been building for years.
It peaked at #49 on the Radio & Records rock chart in the summer of 1994 — modest, but proof the band could reach radio.
Rock veterans Little Feat covered it on their 2000 album Chinese Work Songs — one of the highest compliments a jam band can get.
Hoist's guest list reads like a variety show: Alison Krauss, Béla Fleck, Tower of Power's horn section, even Star Trek's Jonathan Frakes.
This clip comes from The Clifford Ball, Phish's 1996 festival on a decommissioned Air Force base in upstate New York — released as a full DVD.
The studio cut is a tidy 4:39; on stage the song usually stays close to that length — a rarity for this band.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the duo behind most of Phish's best-known songs.

title: Sample in a Jar

description: A hypnotic vocal round from 1990's Lawn Boy — Phish at their most happily lethargic, bouncing off the studio walls.

pops.text: From Lawn Boy, Phish's second studio album — released in 1990 on a tiny indie label, Absolute A Go Go Records.
Elektra Records reissued Lawn Boy in 1992 after signing the band, giving this homemade recording a major-label afterlife.
The song is built as a vocal round — all four members singing the same melody in a canon, each chasing the last.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it turns a surreal dream — bouncing around an empty room — into a pop song.
One reviewer called the studio take a 'tantalizing outtake from some unreleased sessions' — the band at its most masterfully sleepy.
It's the opening track of A Live One (1995), Phish's live album — captured at the Boston Garden on New Year's Eve 1994.
That live version features trumpets, trombones, and saxes — a one-off brass army for a band that's normally a four-piece.
At about three and a half minutes, it's a short breather in concert — the band rarely stretches it into a jam.
Lawn Boy was where Phish learned to use a studio, setting up the far more polished A Picture of Nectar two years later.
Three decades on, it's still a setlist regular — the rare Phish song you could memorize after one listen.

title: Bouncing Around the Room

description: From a three-minute blast to a forty-minute odyssey — the song that became Phish's greatest jam lottery ticket, shown here at their network-TV debut.

pops.text: You're watching history: Phish's first-ever network television appearance, on the Late Show with David Letterman, December 30, 1994.
The song comes from 1992's A Picture of Nectar — the album that got them signed to Elektra Records.
In the early '90s, this was a quick three-minute blast — played and gone.
Then the band discovered it could be stretched into a jam vehicle, and the song's whole destiny changed.
By 2012 it had become a heavyweight: a version in Mexico clocked in at nearly 40 minutes — the longest 'Chalk Dust' ever.
Fans now treat it like a lottery ticket. You never know whether you'll get the short blast or the epic.
The stop-start riff makes it a perfect launchpad — the band argues musically for a while, then lands back together.
It's been played hundreds of times, and its longest versions rank among the biggest improvisations in Phish history.
The title comes from the lyrics — a narrator who can't shake the chalk dust off everything.
From a three-minute single to a forty-minute odyssey — few songs have evolved quite like this one.

title: Chalk Dust Torture

description: Phish's biggest-ever chart hit (#11 Mainstream Rock) — a tight three-minute pop song from the album where a U2 producer taught a jam band to edit.

pops.text: This is Phish's highest-charting single ever — it climbed to #11 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart.
From Billy Breathes (1996), produced by Steve Lillywhite — the U2 and Peter Gabriel producer who made the band cut their jams and focus on songwriting.
It was first played live at a benefit show in Lowell, Massachusetts, where activist Gloria Steinem introduced the band.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was recorded at Bearsville Studios near Woodstock, New York, in early 1996.
Many of the album's ideas came from a songwriting trip the two took to the Cayman Islands — they presented the results on a cassette nicknamed 'King Cayman Baluga.'
The sessions started weird: the band first recorded random notes one at a time in an experiment they called 'The Blob,' using vibraphone, Mellotron, and theremin.
Most of 'The Blob' was scrapped — but a couple of minutes survived inside the album's 'Swept Away' and 'Steep.'
The studio version is a tight 3:48 — one of the shortest songs Phish ever recorded.
The album went Gold in 1999 — Phish's best-selling studio record, and a 2018 vinyl reissue was limited to 7,500 copies.
On stage, 'Free' is a different animal — the band stretches it into a full-throated rock anthem far beyond its three-minute frame.

title: Free

description: The hardest-rocking three minutes of Billy Breathes — Phish's 1996 breakthrough, recorded with more discipline than they'd ever shown.

pops.text: Track two on Billy Breathes — the 1996 album where Phish finally learned to make a proper studio record.
It's a lean 3:58 — producer Steve Lillywhite forced the band to chop their sprawling ideas into tight songs.
Lillywhite came from U2, Peter Gabriel, and the Rolling Stones — the band wanted him to make them sound like a real rock band.
Recording happened at Bearsville Studios in upstate New York, during the first half of 1996.
The sessions began with an odd experiment called 'The Blob' — the band recording single notes at random, one turn at a time.
They reached for vibraphones, a Mellotron, and a theremin. Most of it never made the album.
Billy Breathes was released on Elektra Records in October 1996 and went Gold three years later.
Its lead single 'Free' became Phish's biggest chart hit — #11 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart.
'Character Zero' is the album's hardest-rocking moment — a short, sharp burst of guitar muscle between the ballads.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the pair behind nearly everything on the record.

title: Character Zero

description: A waltz-time refusal of every career except one — wasting time with you — recorded live at Deer Creek in the summer of '96.

pops.text: This version comes from Deer Creek, Indiana, August 13, 1996 — officially released as part of the Live Phish concert series.
The studio original is track three on Billy Breathes, Phish's 1996 Gold record, running 4:49.
It's a waltz-time ballad built on refusal — the lyrics reject one career after another: actor, writer, painter, farmer, outlaw, climber.
All that rejecting lands on one wish: to waste time with you.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was recorded at Bearsville Studios with producer Steve Lillywhite.
Trey turned it into a solo staple, playing it dozens of times alone with an acoustic guitar on his own tours.
Fans sing every word — it's one of the rare Phish songs that works better quiet.
Billy Breathes was the band's sixth studio album, released by Elektra in October 1996.
It's stayed in the rotation for decades — Phish were still playing it at Dick's Sporting Goods Park in Colorado in 2021.
For a band famous for twenty-minute jams, 'Waste' proves they could say everything in under five.

title: Waste

description: The quiet title track of Phish's 2000 album — an aurora-inspired hush that grew out of songwriting weekends in Stowe, Vermont.

pops.text: The title track of Phish's 2000 album — a song inspired by the northern lights.
Trey watched an aurora from a solar flare months before writing it, and the song grew from that memory.
It debuted on Late Night with Conan O'Brien in late 1997 — nearly three years before the album existed.
The song grew out of writing retreats: Trey and Tom Marshall rented houses in Stowe, Vermont and disappeared for long songwriting weekends.
Béla Fleck guests on banjo — he'd been orbiting the band since the early '90s.
It's an acoustic-driven hush of a song — Phish at their gentlest, with the farmhouse sitting on a hill in the lyrics.
The album is named for the song — a rare case of Phish letting one quiet tune define a whole record.
Farmhouse marked the end of an era — the band went on hiatus just months after the 2000 tour wrapped.
The same album gave the band its only mainstream pop-radio hit: the next song in this batch, 'Heavy Things.'
Twenty-five years later, it's still the song Phish reaches for when the night needs to breathe.

title: Farmhouse

description: Phish's one fling with mainstream pop radio — performed at their millennium festival in the Everglades while the crowd chanted 'cheesecake' at the cameras.

pops.text: Phish's only mainstream pop-radio hit — it reached #29 on Billboard's Adult Top 40 in 2000.
This clip is from Big Cypress, their millennium festival in the Florida Everglades — some 85,000 fans, broadcast live on ABC.
During the broadcast, Trey got the whole crowd chanting 'cheesecake' — purely to confuse the TV audience at home.
Elektra picked it as the Farmhouse radio single over rockier options — one writer argued 'Bug' would have been the bigger hit.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was first played by a Trey side project in May 1999.
Phish debuted it that September at the Gorge — one fan wrote it 'blew me away: it's poppy, but in a really cool way.'
A critic later called it 'an instant dud, a soft-rock trifle' — but Phish never cared much about radio.
The band played it on Letterman on May 16, 2000 — the day Farmhouse was released.
Trey once pointed out it shares its chords with the Gamehendge epic 'Icculus' — same skeleton, completely different song.
Still the closest Phish ever got to dentist-office radio — and their fans love it anyway.

title: Heavy Things

description: Mike Gordon's slinky cow-funk showpiece from 2014's Fuego — horns, backup singers, and the funkiest groove on a Bob Ezrin-produced record.

pops.text: This is '555' — the slinky cow-funk centerpiece of Phish's 2014 album Fuego, premiered on YouTube before the release.
It was written by bassist Mike Gordon with Scott Murawski of the band Max Creek — one of the few Phish songs not written by Trey.
Fuego was recorded in Nashville in late 2013 with legendary producer Bob Ezrin — the man behind Pink Floyd's The Wall.
The studio version brings in horns and backup singers — a 'nasty horn section,' as one reviewer put it.
The whole album was road-tested first: Phish debuted all of Fuego live on Halloween 2013 in Atlantic City.
That Halloween show was a 'musical costume from the future' — the album didn't come out for eight more months.
Fuego was Phish's twelfth studio album and their first in five years.
One reviewer joked '555' is '555 times better than Winterqueen' — the mellowest song on the record.
Gordon and Murawski have written together for years — '555' is the funkiest thing their partnership ever produced.
Mike usually sings one or two per album — and when it's his song, the groove always wins.

description: The 4:20 opening blast of 2016's Big Boat — debuted at a tour opener in Oregon and still stretching into second-set launchpad territory.

pops.text: The opening blast of Big Boat (2016), produced by rock legend Bob Ezrin.
Phish first played it live on July 21, 2015 — the opening night of summer tour in Bend, Oregon.
It debuted alongside 'No Men In No Man's Land' — both became setlist mainstays within weeks.
The studio version runs exactly 4:20. So does the album's first single, 'Breath and Burning.' The band has never explained the coincidence.
Listen close: Trey yells 'Leo!' right before the piano solo — his on-mic cue to keyboardist Page McConnell.
The studio band is bigger than four: a percussionist sits in — most likely Andres Forero, the drummer from the musical Hamilton.
Forero also played classical percussion on the album's thirteen-minute closing epic, 'Petrichor.'
Big Boat was recorded on the fly — Nashville, Manhattan, Burlington, even the band members' own houses.
A six-song second set in 2015 — 'Blaze On' into 'Twist' into 'Light' — showed how far the song could stretch live.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the most prolific songwriting partnership in the band's history.

title: Blaze On
